content.text:
Я выбираю **кандидата 4**. Ни один план не просчитан полностью по шагам: это оценка в уме на основе структуры планов, так что вывод приблизительный.

**Как устроены планы.** Каждый план повторяет прогноз со сдвигом на срок поставки. Заказ дня t по товару 0 покрывает спрос дня t+5, по товару 1 — дня t+3. Кандидаты отличаются только тем, на какой коэффициент умножен прогноз.

| Кандидат | Товар 0 | Товар 1 | Примечание |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | ×1,00 | ×1,00 | точно по прогнозу |
| 7 | ≈×1,10 | ≈×1,10 | |
| 1 | ≈×1,10 | ≈×1,15 | |
| 4 | ≈×1,10 | ≈×1,15 | последние поставки ровно по прогнозу |
| 0 | ≈×1,05 | ≈×1,20 | |
| 6 | ≈×1,20 | ≈×1,15 | |
| 5 | ≈×1,20 | ≈×1,30 | |
| 2 | — | — | заказы через день двойными партиями |

**Почему нужен небольшой запас сверх прогноза.**
- Средний множитель спроса около 1,046, поэтому план точно по прогнозу (кандидат 3) систематически недопоставляет.
- Нехватка стоит дороже излишка. По товару 0 недостающая единица обходится примерно в 10 (упущенная маржа 5 плюс неустойка 5). Лишняя единица в основном переходит на следующий день, потому что годность 4 дня, и стоит хранения 0,3 в день. По товару 1 нехватка обходится примерно в 16, а излишек годен 8 дней.

**Почему не больше.**
- У кандидата 5 излишек по товару 1 около 12 единиц в день. Он накапливается: дорогое хранение (0,7 за единицу в день) плюс регулярные списания.
- У кандидата 2 из-за двойных партий через день выше средний запас, а значит, больше хранения и списаний товара 0 при годности 4 дня.
- Разумный уровень — примерно ×1,10–1,15. Это кандидаты 1, 4 и 7.

**Почему 4, а не 1.** До конца у них одинаковые заказы. Но кандидат 4 урезает последние поставки до прогноза: заказы товара 0 с прибытием в дни 27–29 и товара 1 с прибытием в дни 27–29. К концу горизонта уже скопился запас от прежних излишков, и он расходуется вместо новых закупок. Остатки после дня 29 ничего не стоят, поэтому так меньше денег пропадает на непроданный товар.

**Общее для всех планов.** В первые дни нехватка неизбежна при любом плане: стартового запаса (48 и 58) не хватает до первых поставок. Денег хватает на все заказы, урезаний не будет.

**Ответ: кандидат 4.** Но это лучший выбор с умеренной уверенностью, а не явный победитель. Отрыв 4 от 6 и 7 небольшой, при другом исходе случайного спроса порядок между ними может поменяться.

**Как устроены планы.** Почти все кандидаты заказывают каждый день прогноз спроса на день прихода, умноженный на некоторый коэффициент. Заказ товара 0 приходит через 5 дней, товара 1 — через 3.

| Кандидат | Товар 0 | Товар 1 | Особенность |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | ≈1,00 | ≈1,00 | — |
| 0 | ≈1,04 | ≈1,20 | — |
| 7 | ≈1,10 | ≈1,09 | — |
| 1 | ≈1,09 | ≈1,155 | — |
| 4 | ≈1,09 | ≈1,155 | как 1, но в конце заказы ниже |
| 6 | ≈1,20 | ≈1,15 | — |
| 5 | ≈1,20 | ≈1,31 | — |
| 2 | ≈1,10 | ≈1,15 | заказ раз в два дня двойными партиями |

**Кого отбрасываю:**
- **Кандидат 2.** Он экономит фиксированную плату 21 примерно на 13 днях. Но каждую вторую ночь на складе остаётся запас следующего дня: около 30 ед. товара 0 и 50 ед. товара 1. Хранение этого запаса стоит примерно 9 + 35 = 44 за два дня против сэкономленных 21. В итоге он проигрывает дневным планам примерно 300.
- **Кандидат 3.** Средний множитель спроса 1,046, а план заказывает ровно по прогнозу, то есть ниже среднего спроса. Нехватки будут частыми, а это потеря выручки плюс неустойка: 10 на единицу товара 0 и 16 на единицу товара 1.
- **Кандидат 5.** Сильный перезаказ, особенно товара 1. Излишек копится, за него платится хранение 0,7 за единицу в день, а часть ещё и списывается.
- **Кандидат 0.** Товар 0 почти без запаса (≈1,04, тоже ниже среднего спроса), товар 1 с лишним (≈1,20).

**Оставшиеся 1, 4, 6, 7.** Для обоих товаров нехватка обходится заметно дороже излишка. Поэтому заказывать на 10–20 % выше прогноза разумно. Товар 1 хранится 8 дней, так что излишек не пропадает сразу, а становится буфером. Вместимость склада 284 нигде не мешает, даже в пике спроса на товар 1 в день 23.

**Почему 4, а не 1.** Планы совпадают везде, кроме конца горизонта. Остатки в конце ничего не стоят, а у товара 1 к этому моменту уже накоплен буфер. Последние заказы товара 1 у кандидата 4 урезаны до уровня прогноза, это экономит около 24 ед. × 4 ≈ 96. Для товара 0 урезание примерно нейтрально: экономия около 45 против примерно такого же риска нехватки. Значит, кандидат 4 как минимум не хуже 1 и, скорее всего, лучше.

**Почему не 6 или 7.** Кандидат 6 заказывает больше товара 0, кандидат 7 — меньше товара 1. Оба коэффициента лежат в разумном диапазоне, и по средним значениям они почти не отличаются от 4. Перевес кандидата 4 — в грамотно урезанных заказах в конце, которых нет ни у 6, ни у 7.

**Choice: candidate 7.** I estimated this in my head with a rough approximation rather than a full day-by-day simulation, so I'm only moderately confident.

**How the plans differ.** Every plan except candidate 2 is the demand forecast shifted by the delivery lead time (5 days for product 0, 3 days for product 1) and scaled by a constant factor:

| Candidate | Product 0 | Product 1 |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 1.00 (exact forecast) | 1.00 |
| 0 | 1.04 | 1.20 |
| 1 | 1.09 | 1.155 |
| 4 | 1.09 | 1.155, with smaller orders on the last few days |
| 7 | 1.09 | 1.09 |
| 6 | 1.20 | 1.155 |
| 5 | 1.20 | 1.31 |

Candidate 2 orders about the same amounts as candidate 1, but in two-day batches every other day.

Real demand averages about 1.046 × forecast. The first days are short no matter what: product 1 runs out on days 0–2 and product 0 on days 0–4, the same for every plan.

**What a shortage costs compared with a surplus.**
- **Product 1:** each unit of unmet demand costs 20 (13 lost sale + 7 penalty). An extra unit costs 4 to buy and 0.7 a day to store, and anything left at the end is worthless. Leftovers carry over to the next day, so ordering slightly above demand builds a stock cushion.
- I modelled the running stock as a random walk (spread about 90 units over the period) and compared expected shortages, storage and unsold stock:
  - Ratio 1.00: about 113 units short, total cost about 8,680.
  - Ratio 1.09: about 45 units short, total cost about 8,490 (the best).
  - Ratio 1.155: about 24 units short, but storage and end leftovers push the cost to about 9,190 (about 9,090 for candidate 4 thanks to its smaller last orders).
  - Ratio 1.20: about 9,880. Ratio 1.31 is even worse, and the 284-unit warehouse limit is also exceeded.
- **Product 0:** ratios 1.04 and 1.09 come out almost equal (about 4,550–4,590). Ratio 1.00 is slightly worse, and ratio 1.20 is clearly worse (about 4,990) because the excess spoils after 4 days.
- **Candidate 2:** batching saves the 21 order fee on about 13 days (about 273). But half of every batch sits in storage an extra night, about 45 per batch or roughly 590 in total. So it ends up about 300 worse than candidate 1.

**Result.** Candidate 7 gives the most expected profit. It is about 200 ahead of candidate 3 and about 600 ahead of candidate 4, with candidates 1, 0, 6, 2 and 5 further behind. Holding a small cushion also makes it more robust than candidate 3 when demand comes in above forecast. It never reaches the warehouse limit: by the end it holds roughly 110 units of product 1 and 60 of product 0.

**Choice: candidate 4.** I'm only moderately sure it beats candidates 1, 0 and 7. I did the calculation by hand, without a full day-by-day simulation, but the ranking holds up on the main points.

**How the plans line up.** Each day's order is sized to the demand on the day it arrives: 5 days later for product 0, 3 days later for product 1. Candidate 3 orders exactly the forecast. The other daily plans add a fixed markup on top:

| Candidate | Product 0 | Product 1 |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | ×1.00 | ×1.00 |
| 0 | ×1.05 | ×1.2 |
| 7 | ×1.09 | ×1.09 |
| 1 and 4 | ×1.09 | ×1.16 |
| 6 | ×1.2 | ×1.16 |
| 5 | ×1.2 | ×1.3 |

**What the right markup is.** Average demand runs about 4.6% above the forecast, so candidate 3 is short on average and pays the shortage penalty often.
- **Product 1:** a missed sale costs 16 (13 − 4 lost margin + 7 penalty). An unsold unit costs only about 4–5 (purchase price plus storage), and it can still be sold for up to 8 days. A markup of about 1.15–1.25 is right. Candidate 7's 1.09 is too low; candidate 5's 1.3 builds up stock and storage costs.
- **Product 0:** a missed sale costs 10 and an unsold unit about 5, but it only keeps for 4 days. A markup of about 1.1 is reasonable. Candidate 0's 1.05 is slightly low; candidates 6 and 5 at 1.2 are too high.

**Candidate 2 (orders every other day).** It skips 12 order days and saves about 250 in daily fees. But every second day's goods sit in the warehouse one extra night. That costs about 0.7 × 55 + 0.3 × 30 ≈ 47 in storage per two-day cycle, against 21 saved. On top of that, the big product 1 delivery on day 23 (207 units) risks overflowing the 284-unit warehouse. Overall it comes out worse.

**Candidates 1 vs 4.** They are the same plan except for the last few orders. In candidate 4, the orders arriving on days 27–29 are cut to exactly the forecast. Leftover stock is worth nothing at the end, and safety stock has already built up by then. So candidate 4 saves roughly 140 in purchases and gives up few sales. That makes candidate 4 the best of the group.

**Ответ: кандидат 7.** Уверенность умеренная: кандидаты 4 и 3 близки к нему, а мои оценки в уме грубые.

**Как устроены планы.** Почти все кандидаты заказывают каждый день прогноз спроса на день прихода (через L дней), умноженный на свой коэффициент:

| Кандидат | Товар 0 | Товар 1 |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | ×1,00 | ×1,00 |
| 0 | ×1,05 | ×1,20 |
| 7 | ×1,09 | ×1,09 |
| 1 | ×1,09 | ×1,15 |
| 4 | ×1,09 | ×1,15, последние приходы урезаны до прогноза |
| 6 | ×1,20 | ×1,15 |
| 5 | ×1,20 | ×1,31 |

Кандидат 2 устроен иначе: заказывает раз в два дня, по двухдневной партии.

**Кандидат 2 отпадает.** Пропуск заказов экономит около 21 за каждый двухдневный цикл. Но запас на второй день лежит лишнюю ночь: около 50 ед. товара 1 × 0,7 плюс около 27 ед. товара 0 × 0,3, то есть примерно 43 за цикл. Выходит около −22 за цикл, примерно −260 за весь горизонт.

**Товар 1 (годность 8 дней, хранение 0,7).** Средний спрос равен прогнозу × 1,046. Если заказывать больше этого, излишек почти не списывается, а копится на складе.
- При ×1,15 и выше запас растёт примерно на 5 ед. в день. Хранение дорожает с каждым днём, к концу на складе остаются непроданные остатки, а у кандидата 5 возможно переполнение склада (284 ед.).
- От ×1,00 к ×1,09: закупка дороже примерно на 520, хранение примерно на 680. Зато нехватка падает примерно на 55–60 ед., это около +1200 (выручка 13 плюс неустойка 7 за единицу). Итог примерно ничья.
- От ×1,09 к ×1,15: дополнительные затраты на закупку и хранение примерно втрое больше, чем выигрыш на нехватке. Поэтому ×1,15 и выше хуже.

**Товар 0 (годность 4 дня, хранение 0,3).** Нехватка стоит 10 за единицу (упущенная маржа 5 плюс неустойка 5), лишняя единица — 5, излишек частично доживает до продажи.
- ×1,09 немного лучше, чем ×1,00: дополнительная закупка около 300, снижение нехватки около +375.
- ×1,20 уже скорее хуже, чем ×1,09: лишняя закупка около 360, снижение нехватки около +225, плюс больше списаний.

**Почему кандидат 7.** У него наиболее сбалансированные коэффициенты: ×1,09 по обоим товарам. Его ближайшие соперники:
- Кандидат 4 правильно урезает заказы в конце, но весь горизонт держит по товару 1 ×1,15. Лишнее хранение, по моей оценке, перевешивает экономию на конечных остатках.
- Кандидат 3 по товару 1 примерно наравне, но по товару 0 при ×1,00 недозаказывает.

При случайных отклонениях спроса кандидат 7 тоже устойчивее: запас у него не разрастается, как при ×1,15 и выше, и не уходит в постоянную нехватку, как при ×1,00.

I pick **candidate 4**. I compared the plans' order sizes against the forecast estimated in my head, without a full day-by-day simulation, so this is a judgement call rather than a calculated total.

1. **Every plan except candidate 2 orders daily at about forecast × a factor.** A day-t order is sized for the forecast on the day it arrives (t+5 for product 0, t+3 for product 1). The plans differ only in the factor:
   - Candidate 3: about ×1.0 for both products. The average demand multiplier is about 1.046, so stock keeps running down and shortages are frequent. That is costly: each unit short loses margin plus penalty, 10 for product 0 and 16 for product 1.
   - Candidate 7: product 0 about ×1.09, product 1 about ×1.09.
   - Candidates 1 and 4: product 0 about ×1.09, product 1 about ×1.15.
   - Candidate 0: product 0 about ×1.05, product 1 about ×1.2.
   - Candidates 5 and 6: product 0 about ×1.2; product 1 about ×1.3 in 5 and about ×1.15 in 6. Too much product 0: it lasts only 4 days and its margin is low (sells at 10, costs 5), so extra stock gets written off.
2. **A fixed plan needs a buffer.** It does not react to what actually sells, so a surplus over average demand has to absorb random swings (about ±15 units a day for product 1). Product 1 keeps 8 days and costs only 0.7 a day to hold, while a missed unit costs 16. So about ×1.15 for product 1 is a good balance. For product 0, about ×1.05–1.1 is enough.
3. **Candidate 2 orders every other day in double batches.** That saves the 21-per-order fee on 13 days (about 273). But each batch then carries an extra night of storage, about 0.3×30 + 0.7×50 ≈ 44 per batch, which is more than the 21 saved. The plan loses overall.
4. **Candidates 1 and 4 are identical except at the end.** In candidate 4 the orders on days 22–26 are smaller, and those deliveries arrive on days 27–29. Leftover stock is worth nothing at the end, and by then product 1 already has stock built up from earlier surpluses. So cutting the final deliveries saves money and costs almost nothing in sales. Candidate 4 is therefore at least as good as candidate 1, and likely better.

**Choice: candidate 7.** I estimated this rather than simulating it, so it is a reasoned judgement and not a certain one.

1. **All candidates except 2 follow the same pattern.** Each orders the forecast for the day the goods will arrive (day t+5 for product 0, t+3 for product 1), multiplied by a fixed factor. Candidate 3 uses factor 1.0, below the mean demand multiplier of 1.046. Candidates 1, 4 and 7 use about 1.08 for product 0. For product 1, candidates 1 and 4 use 1.15 and candidate 7 uses 1.08. Candidate 0 uses about 1.05 / 1.2, candidate 6 about 1.2 / 1.15, and candidate 5 about 1.2 / 1.3. The start of the month is the same for everyone: initial stock runs out around day 3, before the first deliveries arrive.

2. **Candidate 2 orders every other day.** That saves about 13 order fees of 21 each, roughly 21 every two days. The cost is that the second day's goods sit overnight: about 50 units of product 1 at 0.7 plus about 30 units of product 0 at 0.3, roughly 44. Holding costs more than the saved fee, so batching loses.

3. **The orders don't react to actual sales, so stock drifts.** Each day's surplus or shortfall carries into the next. Daily demand varies by about ±16 units for product 1 and ±8 for product 0, so stock behaves like a random walk.
   - Ordering more each day adds holding cost on the growing stock (about 0.7 × 378/2 ≈ 130). It also leaves more stock at the end, which is worth nothing (≈ 4 × 13.5 ≈ 54).
   - It also reduces shortages, each costing 16 for product 1 (lost 9 margin plus 7 penalty), which saves about 16 × 13.5 ≈ 216.
   - These balance when orders run slightly above mean demand, at a factor of about 1.06–1.1.
   - At 1.15 and above, the extra stock adds about 5 units a day for product 1. Holding then costs well over 1000 more across the month.
   - For product 0, extra stock also expires after 4 days, which costs the purchase price of 5 per unit, so about 1.08 is right there too.
   - Candidate 3, at factor 1.0, gives up on average about 2.4 units of product 1 a day to shortages.

4. **Result:** candidate 7 is closest to the best factor for both products. Candidate 4 is likely second: it matches candidate 1 but trims the last orders. Candidates 5, 0 and 6 over-order the most.

I pick **candidate 1**. I worked this out roughly in my head, not by simulating each plan, so the gaps between the top candidates are estimates.

**How the plans are built.** Seven of the eight plans follow one rule: each day's order equals the forecast for the day it will arrive (5 days ahead for product 0, 3 days ahead for product 1), multiplied by a fixed factor. Candidate 3 uses 1.0. For example, it orders 23 of product 0 on day 0 because the forecast for day 5 is 23. It orders 45 of product 1 because the forecast for day 3 is 45.

| Candidate | Factor, product 0 | Factor, product 1 |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| 7 | ≈1.08 | ≈1.08 |
| 1 | ≈1.10 | ≈1.15 |
| 4 | same as 1, but ends at 1.0 | same as 1, but ends at 1.0 |
| 0 | ≈1.05 | ≈1.20 |
| 6 | ≈1.20 | ≈1.15 |
| 5 | ≈1.20 | ≈1.30 |
| 2 | batches every other day | batches every other day |

**What one unit short or one unit extra costs:**
- **Product 0:** a missing unit costs 10 (5 lost margin + 5 penalty). An extra unit risks a write-off of 5, since it keeps only 4 days.
- **Product 1:** a missing unit costs 16 (9 margin + 7 penalty). An extra unit keeps 8 days and is usually sold later, at 0.7 per day of storage.
- A shortage costs more than a surplus for both products, so ordering somewhat above the forecast pays off. Real demand also averages about 4.6% above the forecast.

**Why candidate 1:**
- **Too lean (3, 7):** demand varies by about ±30% a day, so these run short often and pay 10–16 per missing unit.
- **Too heavy (5, 0, 6):** each day's order runs above average demand, so stock keeps building. For product 0 that means write-offs; for product 1, more storage cost. Candidate 5 has the most surplus. Candidate 0 overloads product 1 and candidate 6 overloads product 0.
- **Candidate 2:** ordering every other day saves the 21 daily fee on about 13 days, roughly 270 in total. But batches that are double size or larger spoil product 0 (4-day shelf life) and push up storage costs. I judged that loss to be larger than the savings.
- **Candidate 4 vs 1:** they are identical except that candidate 4 cuts the last few orders back to exactly the forecast. On the final days, no leftover stock can carry over, so the best order is about 1.29× the forecast for product 1 and about 1.14× for product 0. Cutting back makes shortages more likely, so candidate 4 does slightly worse than candidate 1.

Candidate 1 is in the middle: about +10% on product 0 and +15% on product 1. That covers most of the daily swings without piling up much stock, so I expect it to have the highest profit.

The closest call was between candidate 1 and candidate 6, which differ only in ordering about 10% vs 20% extra of product 0. My rough reckoning favoured 10%, but not by much.

**Pick: candidate 4.** I estimated this by hand without a full day-by-day simulation, so the ranking near the top is approximate.

**What the candidates are.** Every plan except candidate 2 is the demand forecast shifted by the lead time and multiplied by a constant. An order on day t covers demand on day t+5 for item 0 and day t+3 for item 1. The approximate multipliers are:

| Candidate | Item 0 | Item 1 | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 1.00 | 1.00 | |
| 7 | ~1.09 | ~1.09 | |
| 0 | ~1.04 | ~1.20 | |
| 1 | ~1.09 | ~1.15 | |
| 4 | ~1.09 | ~1.15 | same as 1, but the last orders are cut to ~1.0 |
| 6 | ~1.20 | ~1.15 | |
| 5 | ~1.20 | ~1.30 | |

Candidate 2 orders every other day with double quantities, about 1.1 for item 0 and 1.15 for item 1.

**Candidate 2 is worst.** Ordering every other day saves about 12 × 21 ≈ 250 in fixed fees. But half of each double order sits in stock one extra night. That costs about 0.3·30 + 0.7·50 ≈ 44 in storage per cycle, or about 530 over 12 cycles, which is more than the savings.

**How much to order.**
- **Item 0** keeps only 4 days, so leftovers mostly spoil. A shortage costs 10 (lost margin 5 plus penalty 5). Overstock costs about 5 plus storage. The best service level is about 0.67. With the random multiplier that means roughly 1.10–1.14 × forecast. Candidates 1 and 4 (1.09) are closest. Candidate 0 (1.04) orders too little; candidates 5 and 6 (1.2) order too much.
- **Item 1** keeps 8 days, so extra stock carries over to later days and costs only 0.7 per day. A shortage costs 16 (margin 9 plus penalty 7). So it pays to order more, about 1.15–1.2. Candidates 0, 1, 4 and 6 are all in this range. Candidate 5 (1.3) orders too much; candidates 3 and 7 order too little.

**End of the horizon.** Stock left on day 29 is worth nothing, and items arriving on the last days have little time to sell. So the final orders should drop to about the forecast. Candidate 4 does exactly this for the orders on days 22–26: for item 1, 41/55/68 instead of 47/63/78 in candidate 1. Up to that point it matches candidate 1, which already has the best ratios for both items. Candidate 0 keeps item 1 at 1.2 to the end and orders too little of item 0.

**Capacity** (284 units) does not seem to be a real limit for any of the scaled plans.

**Randomness.** Candidate 4's margin of about 9–15% over forecast covers typical swings in demand. It also has less leftover risk at the end than candidates 1 and 0.

I picked **candidate 4**. I worked this out roughly in my head, not with an exact day-by-day simulation, so treat the ranking as an estimate.

**What sets the plans apart**

- **Most plans are the forecast scaled by a constant.** Each order covers the demand on its arrival day (day t + 5 for product 0, day t + 3 for product 1).
  - Candidate 3 orders exactly the forecast (×1.0 for both products).
  - Candidate 0: about ×1.04 for product 0 and ×1.2 for product 1.
  - Candidate 7: about ×1.08–1.09 for both.
  - Candidates 1 and 4: about ×1.09 for product 0 and ×1.155 for product 1.
  - Candidate 6: about ×1.2 for product 0 and ×1.155 for product 1.
  - Candidate 5: about ×1.2 for product 0 and ×1.3 for product 1.
- **Average demand is 1.046 × forecast.** Candidate 3, at ×1.0, is short on average every day. Each missing unit of product 0 costs about 10 (5 lost margin + 5 penalty). Each missing unit of product 1 costs about 16 (9 + 7).
- **Product 1 keeps 8 days, so a moderate surplus pays off.** At about ×1.15, extra stock builds up at roughly 5 units a day.
